b.bio: George (Georg) Phillips, born at Königsberg on 6 September 1804 to an English merchant father (James Phillips) and a Scottish mother (née Hay), studied law at Berlin and Göttingen under von Savigny and Eichhorn and took his doctorate at Göttingen in 1824. He qualified as Privatdozent for German law at Berlin in 1826 and became professor extraordinary there in 1827; he married Charlotte Housselle in 1827. Converted from Protestantism to Catholicism with his wife in 1828 under the influence of K. E. Jarcke, he accepted a call to Munich in 1833 as counsel in the Bavarian Ministry of the Interior, then was named professor of history and shortly after of law at Munich. He later moved to Vienna, where he died on 6 September 1872.
b.s: The work held here is his inquiry into the Pseudo-Isidorian decretals, arguing that the collection is an augmented Spanish compilation whose compiler signed himself 'Mercator' or 'Peccator', that the decretals opposed no existing discipline, and that they assert a divinely instituted Roman primacy joined inseparably to the episcopate — against historians who attributed them to Isidore II of Setabis.

b.bio: The name as printed collides with two figures. The George Akropolites of the sources (1217 or 1220–1282) was a Byzantine historian and statesman, grand logothete under Michael VIII Palaiologos and author of a chronicle covering 1203–1261; nothing in those sources connects him to Latin patristic texts in Migne's PL 62. The works held here belong to a different hand entirely: a dedication letter arguing that peace comes only from divine oracles and that princes image God through justice, and a life of Eugyppius stating he was born at Carthage and educated under Boethius — material from the Vandal-era African church that fought Arian persecutors such as Huneric and Thrasamund. The attribution to Akropolites cannot be reconciled with the sourced biography.
b.s: The two pieces held here are minor Latin texts from the anti-Arian African tradition preserved in PL 62, not the work of the Byzantine chronicler who bears this name.

b.bio: Giles of Paris (Aegidius Parisiensis) was a French poet and theologian, canon of Saint-Marcel in Paris. He is best known for the Carolinus (Karolinus), a mirror-for-princes poem on Charlemagne written around 1200 for the young Louis VIII. He also revised and expanded Pierre Riga's Aurora, a verse rendering of the Bible with allegorical glosses; the library holds fragments from this revised Aurora together with short Latin verses on the punishments of hell. He is not to be confused with Gilo of Toucy (also called Gilo of Paris), the early twelfth-century cardinal-bishop of Tusculum who wrote most of the Historia de via Hierosolymitana, a verse history of the First Crusade.
b.s: His Aurora revision carried Pierre Riga's versified Scripture, with its doctrine that gospel truth dawns beneath the literal sense, into wider circulation.

b.bio: Gabriel de L'Aubespine, printed here as Gabriel Albaspinaeus, was born in Paris on 26 January 1579, son of Guillaume de L'Aubespine, baron of Chateauneuf. In 1604 he succeeded his kinsman Jean de L'Aubespine as Bishop of Orléans, an office he held until his death at Grenoble on 15 August 1630. He was made a knight of the Order of the Holy Spirit in 1619 and was known for his patristic learning, writing on ancient liturgical rites and annotating Tertullian and Optatus of Milevis.
b.s: His Observations on St. Optatus defend Caecilian against Donatist calumnies, argue that schism lies in pertinacity rather than separation, and answer recent writers — including Calvin — who cited Eusebius, Epiphanius, or Theodoret against Optatus's account.

b.bio: No surviving record identifies Josephus A. Amadesius. The three biographical entries retrieved describe different men who happen to share part of the name: Josephus Adjutus (c. 1602–1668), an Assyrian-born theologian born in Mosul/Ninive who was made deacon in 1632, earned a doctorate in theology at Bologna in 1637, and renounced Rome at Wittenberg on 23 October 1643; Amadeus (Amedius) of Portugal (b. c. 1420), the Franciscan João de Mendez, founder of Maria della Pace at Milan; and the 'Josephus Latinus', the medieval Latin Josephus corpus. None wrote on Ravenna's metropolitan status. The library record alone shows what can be said: a polemical historical dissertation, printed among Migne's Latin series (PL 52), defending Ravenna's subjection to Milan against Bacchini and other Milanese writers.
b.s: The single work held here is a 45-page response-dissertation arguing that metropolises arose from apostolic chairs and that Ravenna and Aquileia were subject to Milan, directed against Bacchini and the Milanese authors.

b.bio: Giovanni Cristofano Amaduzzi was born at Savignano sul Rubicone on 18 August 1740 and died in Rome on 21 January 1792. Educated at the Episcopal Seminary in Rimini and a Minorite, he came to Rome in 1762 to study Oriental languages. From 1769 he taught Greek at the Sapienza (and until 1771 also at the Collegio Urbano of Propaganda), and from January 1770 directed the printing press of the Propaganda Fide, where he edited and introduced a series of 'Alphabetum' volumes covering Indian and other Asian scripts — Malayalam/Sanskrit (1772), Tibetan (1773), Burmese (1776), Persian (1783), Armenian (1784), Ethiopic (1789), among others. He was not a patristic author; his appearance under 'Latin Fathers' reflects editorial work on a Migne volume.
b.s: The work held here is his preface to a volume of Patrologia Latina (PL 67), evidence of his role as an editor rather than as an ancient author; readers should treat the volume's contents as patristic texts and the preface as eighteenth-century scholarship.

b.bio: Vossius, Gerard (1577–1649) — Gerardus Joannes Vossius (Gerrit Janszoon Vos) was born in March or April 1577 near Heidelberg, where his father, a Protestant exile from the Netherlands, briefly pastored. He entered the University of Leiden in 1595, becoming a lifelong friend of Hugo Grotius, served as rector of the Latin school at Dordrecht from 1600, and directed the theological college at Leiden from 1614 to 1619. Despite his moderation he came under suspicion of heresy and resigned in 1619 rather than face expulsion. He died in Amsterdam on 19 March 1649. His scholarship spanned philology, church history, and historical theology; his Historia Pelagiana appeared in 1618.
b.s: The library holds his short Life of Saint Ephraem (PL 73), a hagiographical and exegetical account presenting Ephraem's teaching as inspired by the Holy Spirit and his meekness, humility, repentance, and prayer as exemplary for preachers and penitents.

b.bio: Johann Franz Bessel, in religion Gottfried, was born at Buchen in the Grand Duchy of Baden on 5 September 1672 and died at Göttweig on 22 January 1749. He entered the Benedictine Order at Göttweig on the Danube, Lower Austria, on 15 June 1692, studied philosophy and theology at Salzburg and completed his theological course at Vienna, took a Doctorate of Theology in 1696 and later a Doctorate of Juris Utriusque after legal study in Rome, served Archbishop Lothar Franz von Schönborn at Mainz from 1703 as vicar general and supreme judge of the ecclesiastical court, undertook diplomatic missions including three journeys to Rome, was elected Abbot of Göttweig on 7 February 1714, twice served as honorary rector of the University of Vienna (1714/15 and 1726/27), and acted as imperial theologian and diplomat.
b.s: The work held here is his two-page prefatory letter to the Viennese edition printed in PL 33, which surveys citations on original sin, infant baptism, grace, and predestination, dates its subject text before 420 by appeal to the City of God reference, and argues against Optatus, patrons and deniers of the tradux, and the Pelagians.

b.bio: Geoffroy Tory of Bourges was a Paris printer, bookseller, corrector, engraver, and teacher of grammar. He studied at Bourges and in Italy (Bologna), taught at several Paris colleges, and worked as corrector for Gilles de Gourmont and Henri Estienne before setting up as a printer-librarian. In 1530 Francis I named him imprimeur du roi; he died in Paris before 14 October 1533. He is remembered chiefly for Champ fleury (1529) and for promoting roman type and orthographic reform in French printing.
b.s: The two items held here are his prefatory pieces — a dedication letter and an address 'To the reader' — printed with a Latin text in Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL 130); they show the humanist editor's apparatus (citing Priscian, Columella, Plautus) rather than any theological argument of his own.

b.bio: Bianchini, born at Verona in 1704, was a canon of Verona cathedral before entering the Oratory of St. Philip Neri at Rome in 1732. Clement XII and Benedict XIV entrusted him with scholarly commissions, and Benedict XIV named him secretary of an academy; Clement XIII later designated him to continue Baronius's Annals. His major works include the Vindiciae Canonicarum Scripturarum Vulgatae latinae editionis (Rome, 1740), the Evangeliarium quadruplex latinae versionis antiquae (Rome, 1749), the Liturgia antiqua hispanica, gothica, isidoriana, mozarabica, toletana mixta (Rome, 1746), and a fourth volume added to his uncle Francesco Bianchini's edition of Anastasius Bibliothecarius's Lives of the Popes (Rome, 1735).
b.s: The works held here are his textual-critical letters and notices on early Latin Gospel codices — including judgment on the Vercelli Codex — arguing that many distinct early Latin translations of Scripture existed and that recourse to Hebrew and Greek originals resolves variant readings.

Francesco Bianchini (1662–1729) — Born at Verona in the Republic of Venice, educated by Jesuits at Bologna and at Padua under the astronomer Geminiano Montanari, he moved to Rome in 1684 as custodian of Cardinal Ottoboni's library. Alexander VIII made him papal chamberlain and canon of Santa Maria Maggiore; Clement XI made him secretary of the commission for calendar reform and sent him to Paris in 1712. He was elected FRS in 1713, proposed by Isaac Newton, and Benedict XIII appointed him historiographer. He was a deacon but never a priest.
b.s: The works held here are his textual-critical letters and notices on early Latin Gospel codices — including judgment on the Vercelli Codex — arguing that many distinct early Latin translations of Scripture existed and that recourse to Hebrew and Greek originals resolves variant readings.

b.bio: Gaetano Cenni, born at Spignana, died at Rome, was an Italian abbé and paleographer who worked in Rome in the first half of the eighteenth century. He edited the Council of Rome of 769 (1735), wrote on the antiquity of the Spanish church (1740–41), and published the Codex Carolinus and Codex Rudolphinus with a chronology illustrated by dissertations (1760). His dissertations examine imperial diplomas from Louis the Pious through Rudolph, the letters of Leo III, and the charter of Countess Matilda, arguing that Carolingian and later emperors sought and received papal confirmation of their elevation.
b.s: The works held here are his chronological and diplomatic dissertations defending papal involvement in imperial elections and coronations, written largely against Baronius, Pagi, Muratori, and Flacius.

w: Letter for the renewal of the feast of Saint Remigius

b.bio: This entry covers a collective author: the bishops and clergy of the Frankish and later French church, whose corporate acts survive in Migne's Patrologia Latina. The library holds one such act, a letter renewing the feast of Saint Remigius of Reims. It argues that the feast was sanctioned by councils, popes, and kings; that Remigius converted Clovis and thereby founded Frankish Christianity; and that heretical contagion calls for patronal intercession. It cites Pope Hormisdas, the councils of the Gallican church, the supreme pontiffs, and the kings. No individual author or dates can be assigned from the record.
b.s: The letter shows how the Gallican church grounded its liturgical life in conciliar, papal, and royal authority while claiming Remigius as the founder of its national Christianity. More broadly, the national Church of France had a distinctive spirit of freedom toward Rome traceable far back into antiquity (source:3), a spirit of which such corporate acts are expressions.

b.bio: Gilbert Cousin (Latinized Cognatus), born at Nozeroy in Franche-Comté on January 21, 1506, studied jurisprudence at Dole before turning to church service. From 1530 to about 1535 he served as copyist and secretary to Erasmus, who taught him Greek and Latin letters. He became canon of St. Anthony of Nozeroy in 1535 and a teacher there, traveled to Italy in 1558 with Archbishop Claude La Baume of Besançon, and after returning adopted Protestant sentiments. Pope Pius V ordered his arrest for heresy on July 8, 1567. Sources disagree on his death: McClintock and Strong say he died in prison that year; CERL gives Besançon, May 22, 1572.
b.s: The library holds one item under his name, a historical testimony printed in PL 53 that cites Arnobius and Jerome; readers should note it sits oddly beside his known career as Erasmus's secretary and humanist historian.

b.bio:
Giovanni Domenico Coleti (1727–1798/99) — Venetian-born Jesuit, brother of Jacopo Coleti. He studied under the Latinist Camillo Berardi at Ravenna, served as a missionary in South America from 1755 (Cartagena, Panama, Guayaquil, Quito), and was expelled with the order in 1767 by Charles III's decree. After the Society's suppression in 1773 he settled in Italy, working as secretary to Count Gaetano Ginanni of Ravenna and publishing antiquarian and historical works. Sources disagree on his death date: Wikipedia gives 5 January 1798; McClintock and Strong give Venice, 1799.

Giacomo Coleti (1734–1827) — Giovanni Giacomo (Jacopo) Coleti, born in Venice, entered the Society of Jesus and taught at the Jesuit college in Padua from 1768, working with Daniele Farlati. After the suppression of the order he returned to his family and devoted himself to study and ecclesiastical labors, continuing Farlati's Illyricum sacrum through volumes V to IX and publishing the Martyrologium Illyricum (1819). He assisted his brother Giovanni Domenico's edition of Lucifer of Cagliari; the prefatory and biographical pieces held here are his contribution to that edition.
b.s: The works held here are his prefatory and biographical apparatus for the 1778 edition of Lucifer of Cagliari's extant works, defending Lucifer's orthodoxy against Arianism and Constantius while correcting Tillemont and Rufinus on the Council of Milan and the subscriptions against Athanasius.

b.bio: Georg Colvener (Colvenerius), a Flemish theologian born at Louvain in 1564, was provost of the college and chancellor of the University of Douay; he died in 1649. He edited patristic and medieval texts, including the edition of Rabanus Maurus's complete works printed at Cologne in 1617 — the edition from which the library's three pieces under his name are taken. His other editions include Balderic's Chronicon Cameracense et Atrabatense (1615) and Thomas de Cantimpré's Miraculorum et Exemplorum Memorabilium Libri duo (1627). The works held here are not independent treatises but editorial matter: scholia, an explanation of obscure or barbarous words, and a short notice appended to the Rabanus Maurus volume.
b.s: His value to readers of this library is as the learned seventeenth-century editor whose annotations on early Frankish church history — bishops of Reims and Soissons, place-names like Durocortorum and Divodorum, subscriptions at Arles 314 — accompany the text he published.

b.bio: Gisbert Cuper was a Dutch antiquary, philologist, and politician. Sources differ on his birth: the CTHS notice gives 28 September 1644 at Deventer, while the Deutsche Digitale Bibliothek record gives 14 September 1644 at Hemmen in Gelderland; both agree he died at Deventer on 22 November 1716. He taught history and rhetoric at the Athenaeum in Deventer from 1668, became its Rector in 1672, then burgomaster of the city in 1674. As delegate to the States General (1681–1694) he moved to The Hague and left teaching, though he apparently remained active in the Republic of Letters. He was elected an honorary foreign member of the Académie royale des inscriptions et belles-lettres in 1715.
b.s: The works held here are his philological notes on Lactantius's De Mortibus Persecutorum, correcting Valesius, Baluze, Tristan, and Vossius on points such as imperial terminology ('generis humani' as the Roman Empire), the meaning of 'church' as the assembly of the faithful rather than a building, and a conjectural restoration of a lacuna.

b.bio: The name as printed here cannot be identified with confidence from the surviving records. The only Guillaume Desprez documented in them is a Parisian printer-bookseller (c. 1629–1708), apprenticed to Denis de La Nouë from March 1643, received as libraire on 30 March 1651, and the principal publisher of Port-Royal texts including Pascal's Pensées (source:1, source:2, source:3). That man was a tradesman of the seventeenth century, not a patristic author, and no source connects him to a dedication letter printed among the works of Fulgentius in PL 65. The dedication held under this name was therefore written by some other bearer of the name, who remains unidentified here.
b.s: The single item held is a dedicatory letter prefacing Fulgentius's works, asserting that patronage of the fathers edifies the church and that civil and ecclesiastical power mutually support each other.

b.bio: Georg Joseph (von) Eggs, printed here as Georg Joseph Eggsius, was a Catholic theologian of the late seventeenth and eighteenth centuries; Deutsche Biographie gives his dates as 1663–1755 and lists him simply as a Catholic theologian, without further biographical detail in the source consulted. He should not be confused with the composer and organist Georg Joseph Vogler (1749–1814), a different man who shares part of the name. Open Library records one work under his Latinized name, Georgius Josephus ab Eggs: Pontificium doctum, on the lives, deeds, deaths, and other notable matters of the Roman pontiffs.
b.s: The library's holdings under this name are brief historical notices in Migne's Patrologia Latina (vols. 137, 142, 143), not substantial theological works; his separate Pontificium doctum collected material on the popes.

b.bio: Geverhart (Gebhart) Elmenhorst was born in Hamburg around 1580 or 1583 — the sources disagree on the year — to a prominent family; his father, who styled himself Gevert Delmenhorst, served on the city senate. He studied at Leiden under Scaliger's influence and returned to Hamburg in 1602, living as a private scholar devoted to philological and theological study. He edited post-classical Latin authors and early church writers: Arnobius (1603/1610), Minucius Felix (1612), Gennadius (1614), Sidonius Apollinaris (1617), Cebes (1618), and Apuleius (1621). He died in Hamburg in December 1621 without descendants.
b.s: The work held here is his set of notes accompanying his 1614 edition of Gennadius's De dogmatibus ecclesiasticis, a doctrinal compendium covering sin, Christology, the Trinity, sacraments, grace, baptism, the church, and last things, marshalling citations from Augustine, Jerome, Tertullian, Athanasius, Bede, and others against heretics generally, tritheists, Pelagians, and Bellarmine.

b.bio:
Gabelentz, Hans Conon von der (1807–1874) — Hans Conon von der Gabelentz was born at Altenburg on 13 October 1807 and died at Lemnitz on 3 September 1874. A linguist of wide range — Manchu, Finno-Ugric, and other languages — he also pursued a public career in the duchy of Saxe-Altenburg, serving as privy-councillor (from 1843), Landmarschall in Weimar (from 1847), prime minister from November 1848 to August 1849, and president of the duchy's second chamber from 1851 to 1868. He studied at Leipzig and Göttingen; Julius Löbe, cited alongside him in this library's record, was his schoolfellow and later collaborator.

Loebe, J. (unknown) — The library holds under this name a single dedication letter printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL 18), a prefatory piece rather than a patristic text. The letter itself names two men together — H. c. de Gabelentz and J. Loebe — which points to the pair of scholars associated with the modern critical edition of Commodian; no surviving record here gives biographical facts for either, so none are asserted. What can be said rests on the letter's own content: it addresses a prince as the chief patron of letters and argues that monastic libraries preserve treasures that scholarship can still recover.
b.s: He belongs here not as a Latin Father but as a nineteenth-century scholar: the single item held under his name is a dedication letter arguing that princes are the chief patrons of letters and that monastic libraries hold recoverable treasures, reflecting the editorial scholarship he undertook with Löbe.

w: Another life of Charles the Good

b.bio: Galbert of Bruges (Galbertus notarius Brugensis) was a Flemish cleric and a functionary in the count of Flanders's administration at Bruges. He is known for his day-by-day Latin account De multro, traditione et occisione gloriosi Karoli comitis Flandriarum of the murder of Count Charles the Good in 1127 and the civil war that followed, up to Thierry of Alsace's accession in summer 1128. The work held here is a life of Charles the Good printed in PL 166; it treats providence, sin, and the magistrate, asserts that excommunicate traitors are denied absolution and burial and that earthly powers are ordained by God, and argues against Count William, William of Ypres, and other opponents.
b.s: His chronicle is a near-contemporary witness to the murder of Charles the Good and the Flemish succession crisis of 1127–1128, read here for its theology of rulership, betrayal, and divine judgment.

b.bio: Gallus (Gal I) came from a noble Gallo-Roman (senatorial) family of Clermont, descended on his mother's side from the martyr Vettius Apagatus. He entered the monastery of Cournon, was educated and ordained a priest by Bishop Quintianus, and succeeded him in the see of Clermont in 526–527. He was taken prisoner by King Theuderic I during the Frankish invasion of Auvergne and later enjoyed royal favor; as bishop he hosted the Council of Clermont (535) and took part in synods at Orléans between 533 and 549. His nephew Gregory of Tours wrote his Life (Vitae patrum 6), and Venantius Fortunatus composed his epitaph. A later bishop of the same diocese, Gal II, shares the name and is a distinct person.
b.s: The work held here is a single epistle printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina 87; Gallus matters chiefly through Gregory of Tours' Life of him as a model sixth-century Gallic bishop.

b.bio: The library prints this author as Gallus the Irishman, and readers will meet the same Latin name attached to Saint Gall (c. 550–c. 645), the Irish disciple of Columbanus who separated from him in 612 and settled as a hermit in Swabia near Bregenz, on a site that later became the Abbey of Sankt Gallen. But the sources describe that Gall as a missionary monk and hermit, not as a writer, and none of them attributes any sermon to him. The single Sermon held here (PL 87) is therefore best treated as a work printed under his name whose authorship cannot be confirmed from these sources.
b.s: The Sermon here is a short piece of salvation-history preaching: it moves from the creation and fall of the angels through Adam's sin (prompted by Satan's envy), the flood, and Babel to idolatry's origin in the worship of dead men and demons, arguing that elect men fill the number of fallen angels.

b.bio: Galo of Paris is Galon (Galo, Gallon), born in Beauvais, abbot of Saint-Quentin, then bishop of Beauvais from about 1099 to 1104 and bishop of Paris until his death on February 23, 1116. Pope Paschal II appointed him papal legate to Poland around 1103, where he supervised the Gregorian reform, deposed two bishops at a council for violating the canons, and introduced Ivo of Chartres's Collectio trium partium. He was present at the Council of Châlons in 1115. The works held here under his name—a diploma and an epistle in PL 162—cite 'the lord pope Paschal' and 'King Philip and his son Louis,' which matches this man's period and correspondents. A different Galo (died 1129) was a monk of Saumur and bishop of Saint-Pol-de-Léon; Gilo of Toucy ('Gilo of Paris,' died after 1139) was a Cluniac poet and cardinal-bishop of Tusculum. Neither matches these works.
b.s: His two short pieces here are administrative acts of Gregorian-era church government: they assert that pastors must correct immoral subjects or be condemned, that broken chastity vows justify expelling monks, that papal authority authorizes reform of corrupt monasteries, and that episcopal jurisdiction survives a monastery's transfer to another abbot.

w: Names of authors in the book called Verbum abbreviatum

b.bio: Georgius (Georges) Galopinus was a Benedictine religious and librarian at the monastery of Saint-Ghislain in the province of Hainaut. His recorded achievement is the recovery of Peter the Chanter's Verbum abbreviatum from manuscript sources: he first brought the text to light ('e tenebris primus eruit'), and it was printed under his name in Migne's Patrologia Latina (vol. 205, Paris, 1855). The library holds his index to that work and his list of authors named in it.
b.s: He is remembered as the editor who first recovered Peter the Chanter's Verbum abbreviatum; the works held here are his index to that text and his list of the authors cited in it.

b.bio: Garcia was a monk at the Benedictine abbey of Saint-Michel-de-Cuxa in the Pyrenees. He is known for a single letter addressed to Oliba, bishop of Vich and abbot of both Cuxa and Ripoll. In it he describes the abbey church begun in 955 and dedicated in 974 under Abbot Guarinus (Watinus): a nave with side aisles, massive wall-like piers, large well-dressed stones, arches, roof, and rich ornamentation. The letter is cited by architectural historians as evidence for the form and decoration of the pre-Romanesque church.
b.s: His letter to Oliba is a principal contemporary description of the tenth-century church of Cuxa, valuable for the history of the building rather than for doctrine; the theological loci the library mines from its six pages come from that same descriptive text.

b.bio: Nothing in The surviving records concerns this author: they describe Tommaso Garzoni (1549–1589), a Canons Regular of the Lateran and encyclopedic writer of Bagnacavallo, and Leonardo Garzoni (1543–1592), a Jesuit natural philosopher of Venice who wrote on magnetism — different men of similar name. The library record alone shows a Joannes Matthaeus Garzon who edited and annotated the chronicle of Idatius in PL 74, disputing points of late-antique Spanish geography and chronology — the location of Cauca at Coca, its assignment to Gallaecia, the birthplace of Serena, Mela's Duria as a scribal error, and the placement of the sixth rather than fifth year of Marcian. His opponents include Pagi, Noris, Paschasius Quesnel, and Florius.
b.s: His notes on Idatius are a work of chronological and geographical criticism on a key source for fifth-century Spain and the Goths, engaging Pagi, Noris, and Quesnel.

w: On the Acquisition of the Kingdom of Sicily, Calabria, Apulia, and the Island of Sicily

b.bio: Gaufredus Malaterra was an eleventh-century Benedictine monk and historian who came to southern Italy from a region 'beyond the mountains' (usually read as north of the Alps), spent time in Apulia, and entered the monastery of Sant'Agata at Catania under Abbot Angerius after Sicily's conquest by Roger and his brother Robert Guiscard. He says of himself only that he had earlier lived a worldly life before taking up monastic peace; a tradition placing him at St-Évroult in Normandy rests on Orderic Vitalis's mention of him but lacks supporting evidence. His chronicle in four books, De rebus gestis Rogerii Calabriae et Siciliae comitis et Roberti Guiscardi ducis fratris eius, was written at Count Roger's urging.
b.s: The work held here is his four-book history of the Norman acquisition of Sicily, Calabria, and Apulia by Count Roger and Robert Guiscard, framing the Hauteville rise as providential and treating church order, true worship, the civil magistrate, marriage, and rule in the new Norman territories.

b.t: Latin medieval (inferred from inclusion in PL 173)
b.bio: None of The surviving records describes this Geoffrey of Châlons; they cover two other men named Geoffrey — Geoffrey of Clairvaux (Cistercian abbot, secretary to Bernard) and Geoffrey of Vendôme (Benedictine cardinal) — and neither matches the works held here, so they cannot be used for this note. The library's three pages identify him through his own correspondence in PL 173: he writes to William, bishop of Châlons, and mentions Geoffrey, dean of Compiègne, citing Gallia Christiana volume X (instrum. 167, col. 168) for his documents. His letters concern provisions for churches, monastic exemptions under episcopal obedience, protection of ecclesiastical donations by anathema, contemplatives meriting temporal recompense from prelates, private celebration sufficing when priests are few, and a perpetual daily mass in honor of Mary.
b.s: His letters are documentary evidence for relations between bishops and exempt monasteries in the province of Châlons (twelfth century is plausible but not confirmed by any surviving records), not systematic theology.

b.bio: Gaunilo was a Benedictine monk of Marmoutier Abbey near Tours, active in the eleventh century. His only surviving work is the Liber pro insipiente, written shortly after Anselm of Canterbury's Proslogion (1077–78) as a reply to its ontological argument. Anselm answered it in his Responsio and ordered both texts circulated with the Proslogion. Nothing else bearing Gaunilo's name survives. The library prints his name as 'Gaunilo majoris monasterii' — Gaunilo of Marmoutier ('the greater monastery').
b.s: His Book for the Fool is the first sustained critique of the ontological argument, raising by parody — a perfect island no less than God cannot be argued from concept into existence — objections that remain standard.

b.bio: Gauzlin, a natural son of Hugh Capet, was raised at Fleury and became its abbot at the death of Abbo (sources give 1004 or 1005). He was made archbishop of Bourges in 1013 by favor of King Robert (Molinier); McClintock's account of Dagbert's death (1020) and Gauzlin's entry into the see (1014) is internally inconsistent, though it credits Pope Benedict VIII's intervention with enabling him to take possession against local opposition. He attended the Council of Orléans (1022), which condemned the heresiarch Stephen, and the Council of Paris (1024), where the apostleship of St. Martial was debated. André of Fleury wrote his life in two books.
b.s: The works held here are letters treating death as an appointed irrevocable hour for mortals and prayers for the dead as benefiting their souls, plus a sermon on St. Martial relevant to the apostleship dispute he debated at Paris.

b.bio: Gebuin (Gibuin, Jubin), a native of Lotharingia and son of Hugh III, Count of Dijon according to some accounts, was canon of Langres in 1059 and archdeacon by 1068. Elected archbishop of Lyon at the Council of Autun in 1077 with the backing of the papal legate Hugh of Die, he traveled to Rome in 1079 and obtained from Gregory VII a bull of 19 April confirming Lyon's primacy over the provinces of Lyon, Sens, Rouen, and Tours. He died in office on 18 April 1082 and is honored as a saint with a feast day on 18 April.
b.s: The library holds his letter to Rudolph (PL 147), which argues that humility casts down the proud and exalts the lowly, that Christ conquered the devil by humility, and that obedience to mother church binds the faithful together in charity.

b.bio: Giovanni Caetani of Gaeta, a monk of Monte Cassino, was created cardinal by Urban II in 1088 and served as chancellor of the Holy See under Paschal II, whose captivity at the hands of Henry V he shared. Elected pope on 24 January 1118 in a secret conclave held to forestall imperial interference, he inherited the investiture controversy. An imperial intruder was set up against him during his pontificate, and Gelasius spent much of his brief papacy in exile, dying at Cluny on 29 January 1119.
b.s: The letters here are curial documents from the height of the investiture struggle: rulings on the pallium, burial rights, due process against accused bishops, and the duty to shun the emperor's intruded antipope as excommunicate.

b.bio: The library prints this name as 'Gerald of Cahors', but neither source under that exact name matches the work held. The two figures the sources describe are Didier (Desiderius) of Cahors, bishop of Cahors from his ordination on 8 April 630 until his death on 15 November 655, and Gerald of Wales (Giraldus Cambrensis), archdeacon of Brecon, born c. 1146 at Manorbier, educated at the University of Paris, a royal clerk and Latin historian who died c. 1223. The single item held here, a letter addressed to an emperor Frederick that cites the king of France and the marquis of Montferrat, sits in the late twelfth-century political world where Gerald of Wales moved; it cannot be assigned with confidence to either sourced figure on present evidence.
b.s: The library holds one letter to Emperor Frederick (PL 205); its attribution is unsettled, so readers should treat the piece as an anonymous or disputed epistle rather than as the work of Didier of Cahors or Gerald of Wales.

b.bio: Born at Corbie in Picardy, Gerald was a child oblate and later cellarer of Corbie Abbey. Cured of violent headaches, as he believed, through the intercession of St. Adalard, he fostered that saint's cult and directed a biography of him. After a pilgrimage to the Holy Land he served briefly as abbot of Saint-Vincent, Laon, then founded La Sauve-Majeure in 1079 on land given by Duke William VIII of Aquitaine; the abbey was exempt from lay control and subject directly to the Holy See. He died there on April 5, 1095.
b.s: The works here are his hagiographical dossier on St. Adalard of Corbie — a life, a collection of miracles, and a charter on prayers — which promoted Adalard's cult and model monastic obedience and humility.

b.bio: The works held here identify their author as Gerard (Girard), bishop of Angoulême and legate of the holy Roman church, acting in the name of Pope Paschal. the surviving records describe other men named Gerard — a translator of Cremona and a bishop of Toul — none of whom is this person, so nothing about his birth, death, or length of office can be asserted from them. What the record shows is a papal judge-delegate settling disputes over church property: he adjudicates against Herveus, abbot of Redon, and Count Conan of Brittany, rules on interdicts for sacrilege against church property, and orders restitution of property seized without judgment.
b.s: His letters are working instruments of Gregorian-era papal justice, showing how legatine authority enforced claims that princes hold their rule from the pope, that interdict punishes sacrilege against church property, and that violent invasion forfeits contested possession.

b.bio: Gerard of Florennes, bishop of Cambrai as Gerard I, was born around 975 into the high nobility of the Low Countries, son of Arnold, seigneur of Florennes. He studied under Gerbert of Aurillac, served as chaplain to Emperor Henry II, and was named bishop on 1 February 1012. He supported monastic reform in Lotharingia through Richard of Saint-Vanne and founded the Abbey of St John the Baptist at Florennes. In 1024/25 he convened a synod at Arras against anti-sacramental heretics (the Acta Synodi Atrebatensis) and commissioned the Gesta episcoporum Cameracensium, whose third book is his vita.
b.s: The letters held here are episcopal rulings on excommunication, absolution, and burial — that the impenitent excommunicate may not be absolved or buried, that death fixes the soul's state irrevocably, and that the church's binding sentence binds in heaven — written partly against Adalberon of Laon and against the sale of absolution for money.

w: Charter of the foundation of Auchy-les-Moines

b.bio: Gerard II of Cambrai, sometimes called Gerard of Lessines, was probably descended from the lords of Lessines in the County of Flanders. A monk and provost of the abbey of Saint-Vaast under Abbot Adolf, he was canonically elected bishop of Cambrai after the death of Lietbert on 22 or 23 June 1076, received investiture with the symbols of his office from Emperor Henry IV in July 1076, and held the see until his death on 11 or 12 August 1092. He was the thirty-third bishop of Cambrai and the last who was also bishop of Arras. His episcopacy coincided with the opening of the Investiture Controversy between emperor and pope; an account of it survives in the Gesta Gerardi secundi episcopi by a continuator of the Gesta episcoporum Cameracensium.
b.s: The library holds under his name only a charter for the foundation of Auchy-les-Moines, a document treating religion/true worship as history rather than doctrine; he is chiefly remembered as a bishop caught between emperor and pope at the start of the Investiture Controversy.

w: Prologue to the Life of St. Romanus

b.bio: The library's record identifies this author only by his printed name, 'Gerard of Saint-Médard de Soissons'; nothing in the sources or the record confirms he was a monk at Saint-Médard de Soissons. Saint-Médard de Soissons was a Benedictine abbey founded in the sixth century (traditionally 557–560) to house the relics of Saint Medard and later a burial place of Merovingian kings Clotaire I and Sigebert I. His held works are a prose Life of Saint Romanus with its prologue; the record states that a metrical life existed but is lost, that the surviving prose version dates to the time of an earlier Hugh, and that it argues against simoniacs and hypocrites.
b.s: His works here are a hagiographical life of Saint Romanus that treats episcopal election by king and people, almsgiving, and the power of saints' prayer against demons.

b.bio: Born at St-Calais in Sarthe on 12 August 1628, Gerberon took Benedictine vows at Saint-Mélaine in Rennes in 1649, was ordained priest in 1655, and taught philosophy and theology in Maurist houses until his departure from the scholastic method and his Jansenist leanings led his superiors to relieve him of teaching duties. At Saint-Germain-des-Prés he prepared the edition of Anselm of Canterbury printed as PL 158–159, to which the two works held here belong. His defence of Jansenist positions, his antiroyalist stance against Louis XIV's encroachments, and the hostility of the Jesuits forced him to flee France in 1682; he settled in the Low Countries and by 1690 was in Brussels in close contact with Arnauld and Quesnel, before dying at the abbey of Saint-Denis on 29 March 1711.
b.s: The works here are from his Maurist scholarship: an apology for Rupert of Deutz defending orthodox eucharistic presence against Calvinists (against M. Claude) and a letter from the Anselm edition.

w: Letter to Charles, brother of King Lothair

b.bio: Gerbert of Aurillac, later Pope Sylvester II, was born near Aurillac in Auvergne around 945–950 and educated at the monastery there before studying in Spain at Barcelona and under Arabian teachers at Cordova and Seville. He taught at the cathedral school of Reims under Archbishop Adalbero, received the abbey of Bobbio from Otto II in 983, helped raise Hugh Capet to the throne, became archbishop of Reims, and reigned as pope from 999 until his death in Rome on 12 May 1003. The library holds one letter addressed to Charles, brother of King Lothair, from his correspondence during the Lotharingian politics of the 980s.
b.s: The work held here is a piece of Gerbert's extensive political correspondence, valuable for the history of the late Carolingian succession crisis rather than doctrine.

w: Brief exposition of the Gallican liturgy

b.bio: Germanus (Germain) was born near Autun around 496 to noble Gallo-Roman parents. Ordained a priest at Autun, he became abbot of the monastery of St. Symphorian there. In 555, while at Paris on a mission to King Childebert, he was raised to the bishopric of Paris on the death of Bishop Eusebius/Sibelius. As bishop he sought to restrain the Merovingian kings and acted as an important though unsuccessful mediator in their fratricidal conflicts. He died in Paris on 28 May 576 and is venerated as a saint in both the Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches.
b.s: The works held here are liturgical-historical pieces printed under his name in PL 72, chiefly an exposition of the ancient Gallican rite covering two lessons before the gospel (OT and NT), the reading of martyrs' acts at their festivals, the responsory of the three children, and the carrying of the reserved sacrament to the altar after the dismissals.

b.bio: Gervase of Reims, also called Gervais de Château-du-Loir, was born at Château-du-Loir in Sarthe around 1007 or 1008 and died on 4 July 1067. Raised by his maternal uncle Avesgaud de Bellême, he succeeded him as Bishop of Le Mans in 1036 and was translated to the archbishopric of Reims in 1055 by Henry I of France. Geoffrey of Anjou imprisoned him for seven years until Pope Leo IX threatened excommunication at the synod of Reims in 1049. As archbishop he crowned Philip I in 1059 and served as regent with Baldwin V of Flanders until 1066.
b.s: The works held here are diplomas and letters from PL 143: charters granting tithes and perpetual altar rights to canons with reversion clauses excepting the grantees' fault, asserting clerical exemption from archdeacons under an abbot's cura animarum accountable to God, and attaching anathema to violation of ecclesiastical decree — documents of eleventh-century episcopal administration rather than theological treatises.

w: On the State of the Church

b.bio: The library prints 'Gilbert of Luni'; the sources identify him as Gilbertus Lunicensis (also Lumnicensis or Limericensis), i.e. Gilbert of Limerick, also called Gilla-Easpuic and formerly abbot of Bangor. Deutsche Biographie dates his life 1070–1145; Migne's Patrologia Latina assigns his writings to 1110–1139, presumably his activity as author. He was a bishop in Ireland who wrote on ecclesiastical order and liturgical use.
b.s: His De Statu Ecclesiae maps the church's hierarchical orders onto the sevenfold Spirit and treats baptism and eucharist as the means by which the faithful pass to heaven, while his letter to the Irish bishops argues against divergent Irish liturgical customs.

b.bio: Gilduin was a Parisian canon regular who became prior and then abbot of Saint-Victor in Paris, holding that office from 1113 until his death on 13 April 1155. He appears in the sources chiefly as the recipient of a manuscript now in the Bibliothèque Mazarine (Ms 47) and as the editor under whose auspices the works of Hugh of Saint-Victor were collected. The library holds one page of his letters, addressed to King Louis of the Franks and Theobald, bishop of Paris, defending the conversion of secular churches to monasteries.
b.s: His letters here are administrative evidence for twelfth-century monastic claims on church property: that religious men rejoice in others' holiness, that converting secular churches to monasteries is lawful, and that alienated church revenues require compensation.

w: History of the Miracles of Saint Amand

b.bio: Gilbert entered the monastery of Elnone (Saint-Amand) near Tournai before February 1066 or 1067, when fire destroyed the abbey; he had earlier been raised to the priesthood and the dignity of dean of the church of Saint-Andrew within the monastery. After the fire, relics of Saint Amand were carried through towns and countryside from June to July of that year to raise funds for rebuilding, and Gilbert was one of the monks who accompanied them. The claim by Casimir Oudin that he became abbot is unsupported.
b.s: His History of the Miracles of Saint Amand records that relic procession through France and defends the healings worked at the saint's relics against skeptics who dismissed the cult as vulgar rumor.

w: Epitome of the Life of Abbot Hugh of Cluny
History of the Deeds of the Jerusalem Journey of Our Time
History of the Way to Jerusalem

b.bio: Gilo of Paris, also called Gilo of Toucy or Gilo of Tusculum, was born in Toucy in the county of Auxerre and lived in Paris before becoming a monk at Cluny. A priest first, he was made cardinal-bishop of Tusculum between 1121 and 1123 and served as papal legate four times: to Poland and Hungary around 1124, to Carinthia in 1126, to the Crusader states in 1128 or 1129, and to Aquitaine from 1131 to 1137. He sided with Antipope Anacletus II in the schism of 1130 and was deposed by the Second Lateran Council in 1139.
b.s: He wrote most of the Historia de via Hierosolymitana, the earliest Latin verse epic of the First Crusade, running from the siege of Nicaea to Godfrey's election at Jerusalem, plus a prose life of Abbot Hugh of Cluny and legatine letters.

w: From the History of the Church of St. James of Compostela

b.bio: The library prints this author as 'Giraldus Compostellana' and holds under his name a history concerning the Church of St. James of Compostela from PL 151. No surviving record treats this author; the sources describe Giraldus Cambrensis (Gerald of Wales), a different medieval writer of a similar Latin name, and must not be used for this entry. No source here gives dates, birthplace, or office for the Compostela author.
b.s: The single work held is a Latin ecclesiastical history centered on the church of St. James at Compostela, treating the locus of the Church.

b.bio: the surviving records describe other men entirely: Theodulf of Orléans (d. 821), the Dominican Reginald of Orléans (d. 1220), and the grammarian Gabriel Girard (1677–1748). None of them is the author of the epitaph printed under this name in PL 141. The library record alone identifies this Girard: a Latin writer credited with an epitaph for Hugh the Great, a tenth-century magnate of the Frankish kingdom. Nothing in the sources establishes his dates, office, or life.
b.s: The single work held here is a verse epitaph on Hugh the Great, a document of tenth-century commemoration.

w: Letter to Matthew on various questions

b.bio: Gilbert de la Porrée, also called Gilbert of Poitiers or Gilbertus Porretanus, was born in Poitiers and studied under Bernard of Chartres at Chartres and under Anselm of Laon at Laon. He taught logic and theology at Chartres, serving as chancellor of the school from 1126 (sources differ on whether he held the office until 1137 or 1140), and lectured in Paris, where John of Salisbury was among his hearers. Named Bishop of Poitiers in 1142, he defended his doctrine of the Trinity against Bernard of Clairvaux's objections before Pope Eugene III at the Councils of Paris (1147) and Reims (1148); the dispute ended without a definite verdict. He died in 1154.
b.s: The works held here are his commentaries on Boethius' theological treatises, his On the Six Principles, and a Letter to Matthew on various questions; they apply rigorous logical distinction to Trinitarian and Christological questions, arguing that personal names are predicated relatively rather than substantially and opposing Nestorian and Eutychian readings.

b.bio: Glycerius was comes domesticorum under Olybrius and was proclaimed Western emperor at Ravenna in March 473 by Gundobad. The Eastern emperor Leo I refused to recognize him and sent Julius Nepos against him; Glycerius abdicated on 24 June 474 without a fight. Sources disagree on his subsequent see: Marcellinus Comes and Paulus Diaconus place his ordination at Portus, while Evagrius says Nepos made him bishop of Salona; he is said to have died after 474, possibly in 480.
b.s: The library holds an imperial edict of Glycerius from PL 72, a rare surviving act of one of the last Western emperors before the fall of the line in 476.

w: Charters of the Commune of Amiens

b.bio: Godfrey (Geoffroy) of Amiens was born in 1066 in the diocese of Soissons and educated from childhood at the Benedictine abbey of Mont-Saint-Quentin, where he was ordained priest at twenty-five. He became abbot of Nogent-sous-Coucy in Champagne around 1096, rebuilding the house, and in 1104 was compelled to accept the bishopric of Amiens, chosen partly for his skill in business affairs. As bishop he enforced clerical celibacy and combated simony; his severity made him unpopular, and his successor at Nogent, Guibert, judged his episcopal performance weaker than his promise. He attempted to resign to La Grande Chartreuse but was recalled by his archbishop and died on November 8, 1115.
b.s: The works held here are not theological treatises but his letters, diplomas, and charters concerning the abbey of Saint-Martin-des-Champs: grants such as the allod of Harbonnières, canonical dispensation of church goods, excommunication of those who seize church property, and episcopal rights reserved against monastic encroachment.

b.bio: Godfrey of Bouillon, son of Count Eustace II of Boulogne and Ida of Lower Lorraine, was Duke of Lower Lorraine from 1089 and a leader of the First Crusade. After the capture of Jerusalem in July 1099 he declined the title of king and ruled as Advocatus Sancti Sepulchri until his death there on 18 July 1100; his brother Baldwin succeeded him as king. He is not a church father or theologian: the library's shelf places him under Latin Fathers only because the Patrologia Latina volume (PL 155) holds his charters. The four items here are administrative and diplomatic texts — the Assizes of Jerusalem attributed to his rule, diplomas, letters, and an address to the crusading army.
b.s: The works here are the founding legal documents of the Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem — assizes said to originate under Godfrey, derived from French customs and usages, later codified by John of Ibelin around 1250 and reviewed under John of Lusignan in 1369 — governing fief-holding, summons, and service obligation.

b.bio: Godfrey of Rheims was born in Rheims and educated at its cathedral school. Archbishop Manasses I appointed him chancellor of the school in 1076 or 1077; he kept the post after Manasses was deposed in 1080, holding it until his death around 1094, after which a charter names a new chancellor. Most of what is known comes from poems in praise of him by his friend Baldric of Dol. Four Latin poems survive, showing the influence of Virgil and Ovid; Williams classifies him as an eleventh-century humanist closer in spirit to the Italian humanists of the Quattrocento than to most contemporaries.
b.s: The work held here, The Dream (PL 160), belongs to his small surviving corpus (four poems) and makes Godfrey an early example of a scholar reviving classical poetic traditions before the twelfth-century renaissance.

b.bio: Godfrey of Viterbo was educated at Bamberg, where Lothair took him in 1133, and served as chaplain to Conrad III before spending some forty years as notary to Frederick I Barbarossa, who sent him on diplomatic missions across Europe, including over forty trips to Rome. He was rewarded with lands at Viterbo, probably in 1169, lived much in Italy, and spent his last days there; the year of his death is not ascertained. In the politico-ecclesiastical conflicts of his time he sided with the emperor without declaring himself hostile to the pope, blaming Hadrian for the schism. (These biographical details rest on the sources; the library record cautions that the notary Godfrey may be a different person from the historian.)
b.s: The library holds a chronicle under PL 198 whose title, per the library record, is Memoria saeculorum rather than Pantheon. It treats chiefly of the church and civil magistrate, argues that persecution brings divine retribution, and dismisses pre-Christian chronicles as fables useless to scholars.

b.bio: Godehard (also Gotthard or Gothard) was born about 960 in Upper Bavaria, near Niederaltaich in the diocese of Passau. Educated at Niederaltaich and at Salzburg, he received the Benedictine habit in 991, became abbot of Niederaltaich in 996, and carried out monastic reform at Tegernsee, Hersfeld, and Kremsmünster. Consecrated bishop of Hildesheim on 2 December 1022 as successor to Bernward, he enforced Benedictine observance in his cathedral chapter and built schools for the education of youth. He died in 1038 and was canonized by Innocent II in 1131.
b.s: The letters held here show a tenth-century reforming abbot-bishop defending monastic discipline: that monks may elect their own abbot, that cohabitation of men and women religious is impermissible, and that summoned religious must answer their bishop personally — written against Theodulus and the bishop of Passau.

b.t: Catholic (recorded by Deutsche Biographie); Tegernsee was a Benedictine abbey, though the sources state only 'katholisch'
b.bio: The library prints the name as Gosbert; the sources give it chiefly as Gozbert (also Gosbert, Gozpert). Three medieval men bear this name and must be kept apart: Gozbert of Saint Gall (abbot there 816–837, also abbot of Rheinau until his death, 4 April 850?), a St. Gosbert who was a Benedictine bishop of Osnabrück (d. 859), and Gozbert of Tegernsee, documented from 975 and dead in 1001. The work held here, an acrostic poem printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 129, cannot on present evidence be securely assigned to any one of these namesakes.
b.s: His single held work is an acrostic poem of devotional exegesis asserting that tearful prayer surpasses worldly delights, that love of God outweighs the wealth of kingdoms, that eternal life is the highest beatitude, and that faithful fighters are written in the book of glory, citing Paul and the Lord Jesus.

w: Greater life of Saint Augustine of the English
History of the Translation of St. Augustine of the English
Lesser life of Saint Augustine of the English

b.bio: Goscelin (also printed as Goscelin of Saint-Bertin or Goscelin of Canterbury) was a Benedictine monk and hagiographer born in Flanders or Brabant around 1035–1040. Sources differ on his birth year: the Oxford Dictionary of National Biography gives c. 1035, Wikipedia c. 1040. He was a monk of St Bertin's at Saint-Omer before coming to England, where he served in the household of Herman, bishop of Ramsbury, and spent the rest of his life visiting monasteries and cathedrals collecting materials for lives of English saints. He was at Ely about 1082 writing on St Etheldreda, at Ramsey between 1087 and 1092 compiling the life of St Ivo, and at Canterbury from 1098, where he wrote his account of the 1091 translation of St Augustine's relics, dedicated to Anselm.
b.s: The works held here are his hagiographies and translation histories — accounts of English saints whose bodies God preserves incorrupt — arguing that divine providence guards relics, that episcopal authority sanctifies opening tombs, and that visions and sweet odors attest hidden saints, against disparagers of unknown saints and simoniacal clergy.

b.bio: Gozbert (also printed Gosbert, Gozpert), a Benedictine from a noble family with estates at Essing near Kelheim, was educated at Augsburg; around 975 he made a donation to St Emmeram in Regensburg and entered that abbey under Abbot Ramwold as a cathedral cleric of Essing. In 982 he became abbot of Tegernsee and brought the Gorzer reform to flower through ties with St Emmeram, St Mang at Füssen, St Pantaleon at Cologne and St Burkard at Würzburg; he had classical authors copied, renewed and enlarged the library and archive, and made the school famous under Froumund and Meginhelm. His friendships with Duke Henry (later Emperor Henry II), Empress Adelaide, who supported his reform as his 'amicissima domina', and Wolfgang of Regensburg helped raise Tegernsee to spiritual and economic height.
b.s: The letters held here are Ottonian monastic correspondence: petitions and exhortations securing perpetual prayer, annual masses and vigils for departed souls, and written remembrance of the abbey's benefactors, citing St Quirinus and Empress Adelaide.

w: Dissertation on the Camaldolese Institute of Peter Damian and the Avellanites

b.bio: Born Francesco Lodovico Grandi at Cremona in the Duchy of Milan; he entered the Camaldolese novitiate at Ferrara around 1687, taking the name Guido, studied philosophy and theology at St. Gregory the Great in Rome from 1693, and taught philosophy for the order at Florence before holding chairs at Pisa. He is remembered chiefly as a mathematician — professor of mathematics at Pisa from 1714 and a Fellow of the Royal Society (1709), known for work on series and the rose curve — but he also wrote on Camaldolese history, including the Martyrologium Camaldulense and Dissertationes Camaldulenses.
b.s: The dissertation held here defends the Camaldolese identity of Peter Damian's institute at Fonte Avellana against Laderchi, Fortunius, and Ughellus, arguing from converging witnesses that Damian was Camaldolese and that the Avellanite monastery produced many saints, including four cardinals.

b.bio: Gregory of Catino was a monk of the Abbey of Farfa, born in 1060 into the family of the counts of Catino, a town near the abbey. His father Dono entered him and his elder brother at Farfa as child oblates; he was educated in the abbatial school founded by Abbot Hugh and remained resident there for life. In 1092 he proposed to Abbot Berard II a full reorganization of Farfa's archives, and from 19 April that year copied every charter, producing by Berard's death in 1099 a two-volume collection he titled Liber gemniagraphus sive cleronomialis ecclesiae pharphensis, known as the Regestum Farfense. Between 1099 and 1103 he compiled a collection of canon-law excerpts for its introduction.
b.s: The works held here are his prefaces to the Farfa cartulary and his register: documents defending Farfa's rights through transcribed charters, framed by arguments on sacred places, saints' patronage, and voluntary exile as imitation of Abraham's faith.

b.bio: Gregory III, son of a Syrian named John, was elected pope by acclamation on 11 February 731 and consecrated after confirmation by the Byzantine exarch at Ravenna — the last pope to seek that approval. His pontificate was marked by the Iconoclastic Controversy under Emperor Leo III, whom he remonstrated with by legates and letters, and by two Roman synods in 731 condemning image-breaking. He also faced the Lombard advance, appealing to Charles Martel for aid without success.
b.s: The works held here are his letters: they show an eighth-century pope governing the western church through canonical discipline — granting the pallium with archiepiscopal rank (worn only at mass and episcopal consecration), ordering rebaptism where baptism was performed by pagans or is doubtful, correcting erring clergy by canonical censure, and defending against Liutprand and Hilprand, kings of the Lombards.

w: Letter to the bishops of the kingdom of the Franks

b.bio: Gregory IV was a Roman, son of John, cardinal priest of the Basilica of St Mark before his election to the papacy near the end of 827; imperial approval from Louis the Pious delayed his consecration until March 828. He died on 25 January 844. His pontificate was dominated by the Carolingian dynastic quarrel between Louis the Pious and his sons: he supported Lothar's revolt against Louis in 833, an intervention that damaged his standing with the Frankish clergy. He also promulgated the Feast of All Saints (1 November) and conferred the pallium on Ansgar.
b.s: The letters held here are decretal correspondence asserting papal jurisdiction — deposition without canonical crime is invalid, fallen clergy restored on penitence, fugitive bishops may serve vacant sees, and monasteries exempted from episcopal control by papal privilege — addressed against Frankish episcopal resistance.

w: Rubrics for the collection of canons

b.bio: Born at Rome around 540 to a wealthy patrician family; served as prefect of Rome before turning his family estate on the Caelian Hill into a monastery. In 579 Pope Pelagius II sent him as papal ambassador to Constantinople, and he became Bishop of Rome on 3 September 590, holding the see until his death on 12 March 604. His administration, correspondence, and reform of Roman worship shaped medieval Christianity; Eastern tradition calls him Gregory the Dialogist after his Dialogues. The two items held here under his name are short pieces from a later canonical collection (PL 163): rubrics for gathering canons and a dedicatory letter.
b.s: The works here preserve teaching on church order — that no bishop may be called universal, that presbyter and bishop were originally one order, and that ordination requires consent — positions drawn on by later canonists and reformers alike.

b.bio: John Gratian, archpriest of St. John at the Latin Gate in Rome, paid Benedict IX to resign and was elected pope on 1 May 1045. Accused of simony in the transaction, he was deposed/resigned at the Council of Sutri on 20 December 1046 before Emperor Henry III and retired to Germany with his chaplain Hildebrand, the future Gregory VII. Sources disagree on his death: late 1047 (Britannica) or early 1048 at Cologne (Catholic Encyclopedia).
b.s: His brief, scandal-marked pontificate prompted imperial intervention that opened the way for the Gregorian reform; the privileges here show him granting monastic rights against secular despoilers.

b.bio: Alberto di Morra was born at Benevento around 1100/1105 to a noble family. He became a monk—sources differ on whether Cistercian or Benedictine—and later a Premonstratensian canon at St Martin's Abbey in Laon; he also taught canon law at Bologna. Adrian IV made him cardinal-deacon of Sant'Adriano in 1156, and Alexander III appointed him Apostolic Chancellor in 1172. Elected pope at Ferrara on 21 October 1187 after Urban III's death, he reconciled the papacy with the Holy Roman Empire, launched the Third Crusade after Saladin's capture of Jerusalem, and died at Pisa on 17 December 1187 after less than two months in office.
b.s: The library holds his letters and privileges from PL 202, which treat the Church, worship, sacraments, and the civil magistrate, and include rulings against bishops and princes exacting payments and against laymen taking tithes.

w: Dedication for Future Memory of the Matter

b.bio: Ugo Boncompagni, born at Bologna on 7 January 1502, studied and later taught jurisprudence at the University of Bologna, served Paul III as a jurist at the Council of Trent, held curial offices under Julius III and Paul IV, was made cardinal by Pius IV in 1565, and reigned as Pope Gregory XIII from 13 May 1572 until his death at Rome on 10 April 1585. He promulgated the Gregorian calendar and founded seminaries. Note on attribution: the two items shelved here under his name stand in PL 187, a volume of twelfth-century papal material, and their theses — that Gratian's Decretum is corrupt and needs emendation, that notarized copies carry the same faith as originals, and that the pope may authorize authoritative editions of church law — belong to that earlier legal milieu, not to the sixteenth-century pontiff described by the sources. the surviving records cover only Boncompagni; they do not establish him as author of these pieces.
b.s: The works held here are brief Latin texts on the authority of church law and the standing of Gratian's Decretum; their attribution to Gregory XIII is doubtful, since the sourced Gregory XIII belongs to the sixteenth century while PL 187 preserves twelfth-century material.

b.bio: Grimoaldus was Archpriest of Pontecorvo in Italy and is venerated in the Roman Catholic Church, with a feast on 29 September. He is believed to have been of English descent. Two other medieval and early modern figures named Grimoald or Grimald appear in the sources — Nicholas Grimald, the sixteenth-century English poet, and Grimaldo de San Millán, the eleventh-century Benedictine hagiographer — but neither matches this author's placement among the Latin Fathers.
b.s: The library holds only a brief appendix under his name in PL 87; he is remembered chiefly as a locally venerated Italian saint rather than as a doctrinal writer.

w: Life of St. Lucius, Pope and Martyr

b.bio: Guaiferius (also printed Waiferius) was a monk of Monte Cassino. The sources give no dates for him; the earliest surviving witness to his works is the eleventh-century Cassino manuscript 280 (datable 1001–1100), so he belongs to that period or earlier. He wrote Latin hagiography and verse: a Vita of Pope Lucius I (BHL 5022), a Carmen on Secundinus venerated at Troyes (BHL 7557), and a Carmen de miraculo on James the Greater (BHL 4078). His verse on Secundinus closes with the line 'Pars vacet ut numquam laudis utraque tuae.'
b.s: The works held here are his hagiographic lives and poems — the Life of St. Lucius, poems, and the Life of Saint Secundinus — which present martyrdom as consecrated spiritual warfare and assert the primacy of Peter and the authority of the Roman pontiff over secular power.

b.bio: Gudinus of Luxeuil is known to Migne's Patrologia Latina by a single work, a rhythmic lament (Rhythmicus), assigned there to the eleventh or twelfth century. The poem mourns a dead wise man — the record names Constantius as head of the schools of Luxeuil and cites King Robert and Abbot Milo (as well as Henry and Gudinus himself) — and treats prayer, eternal life, the company of the saints enjoyed by the departed soul, and forgiveness of sins through Christ's grace. No biographical details beyond this attribution are established.
b.s: His sole surviving work is a versified funeral lament from Luxeuil that pairs grief over creation with doctrinal claims about the soul after death.

w: Ancient statutes of the Church of Lyon

b.bio: Guichard of Pontigny was a Cistercian monk who became abbot of Pontigny in 1137 and hosted Thomas Becket there in 1164. In 1165 Louis VII and Pope Alexander III installed him as Archbishop of Lyon against the imperial candidate Dreux de Beauvoir. He concluded the permutation of 1173 with Count Guy II of Forez, by which the count's rights over Lyon passed to the archbishop, confirmed by a bull of Alexander III, and undertook construction of the new cathedral of Lyon and its great cloister. A different Guichard/Wichard of Lyon, a canon and Latin poet, wrote a satirical poem on monks; that is not this author.
b.s: The library holds his Ancient statutes of the Church of Lyon (PL 199), a defense of the lyonnais church's old customs: it argues that reform restores the ancient fathers' institutes rather than inventing novelties, that memory requires written record, and that negligent or powerful canons who despise church order deserve severe discipline.

w: Charter granted to the Abbey of Corbie

b.bio: Guy, son of Enguerrand I, Count of Ponthieu, was educated at the abbey of Saint-Riquier and was an archdeacon by 1045. As representative of Bishop Fulk II he went to the papal curia in 1049 to press charges against the abbot of Corbie; succeeding Fulk as bishop of Amiens in 1058, he inherited that quarrel and was eventually suspended by Pope Alexander II. He witnessed the crowning of Philip I at Reims in 1059 and wrote the Carmen de Hastingae Proelio celebrating the Norman victory of 1066.
b.s: The works held here are his episcopal letters and charters from the Corbie dispute, asserting episcopal authority over monastic establishments and the necessity of clerical confirmation for valid acts — documents of eleventh-century church-state and bishop-abbey conflict rather than theology proper.

w: Corrective Treatise on Many Errors in Gregorian Chant
Letter to Michael the monk on unknown chant
Micrologus on the Discipline of the Art of Music
Verses on the Explanation of Music

b.bio: Guido of Arezzo (Guido Aretinus) was a Benedictine monk and music theorist. His birthplace is disputed: Britannica says around 990 in Arezzo, while the Catholic Encyclopedia, following Dom Morin, says near Paris at Saint-Maur-des-Fossés around 995. By around 1013 he was teaching at Pomposa Abbey, where his new teaching methods drew resentment from his colleagues; he moved to Arezzo around 1025 under Bishop Tedald's patronage to train cathedral singers. Pope John XIX summoned him to Rome, but illness cut the visit short. The record of his later life is thin; the Catholic Encyclopedia gives his death as 1050 at Avellano near Arezzo.
b.s: The works held here are his practical treatises on chant and notation — the Micrologus, rules and letters on singing unknown chant at sight, monochord division, and corrections of singers' errors — which made him the most influential writer on music between Boethius and Tinctoris.

b.bio: None of surviving records describes a 'Guido Cariloci.' The sourced names are near-homonyms from other periods and professions: Guido delle Colonne (13th-century Sicilian jurist and poet), Guido Carocci (19th-century Florentine historian), Guido Panciroli (16th-century legal antiquarian), and Giovanni Carli (15th-century Dominican). None fits a Latin patristic or medieval author in PL 181, so nothing can be asserted about this person's life, dates, or offices.
b.s: The library holds one work under this name, On Correction (PL 181), but the author's identity cannot be established from the sources at hand.

w: On the Restitution of Manuscripts to Monasteries
Statutes for reconciling peace among Christians

b.bio: Guy II was bishop of Le Puy in the late tenth century, succeeding his brother Drogon in the see in 985 and dying in 996. Earlier he had held several abbeys and benefices; when the Church forbade plural offices, he resigned them and returned what he had taken from monasteries, keeping only the abbey of Carmeri. The works printed under his name in PL 137 are conciliar statutes from the Aquitanian Peace of God movement, which the sources do not describe in detail.
b.s: The pieces held here are Peace of God legislation: statutes protecting churches, forbidding clerics to bear arms and the sale of baptism, binding excommunication to breaches of sworn peace, and requiring restitution of wrongfully seized goods before repentance is accepted.

b.bio: The library prints this name as 'Guy of Sens', but the work held here—a letter to Pope Gregory VIII defending the bishop of Laon against his accusers—belongs to Guy of Bazoches (Guido de Basochis), a French cleric and canon of Châlons-sur-Marne in Champagne, born before 1146 and dead by 1203. He took part in the Third Crusade in the retinue of Henry II of Champagne and wrote as a chronicler, poet, and prolific letter writer; his Liber epistularum was edited by Herbert Adolfsson in 1969. The other 'Guy' figures in the sources—a mid-5th-century grammarian-bishop of Sens (Agroecius), an 11th-century bishop of Amiens—are different men and do not match this record.
b.s: His surviving correspondence, including the letter held here, is a primary source for ecclesiastical politics in twelfth-century France and for the defense of a bishop against charges of misconduct.

b.bio: Guido de Castellione appears in the library's record only as the name attached to three pages of diplomas printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina 142. These documents concern the church of Reims: grants of altars exchanged for prayers for donors, masses and almsgiving for the dead, hereditary rights to altars, anathema against violators of ecclesiastical grants, and a dispute involving Aebalus, Archbishop of Reims. No surviving record identifies this person's dates, office, or biography. the surviving records describe other men named Guido — the canonist Guido de Baysio (d. 1313), Pope Celestine II (born Guido di Castello, d. 1144), and Guido de Monte Rochen (fl. c. 1331) — none of whom matches works of this kind, and they are set aside as homonyms.
b.s: The diplomas held here are documentary evidence for how altar rights, commemorative prayer for donors, and sanctions of excommunication were negotiated between lay patrons and the church of Reims.

b.bio: Gumpold, bishop of Mantua, is attested in that office between 966 and 981. The library holds one work under his name: the Vita Vencezlavi ducis Bohemiae, a Latin life of Duke Wenceslaus of Bohemia, printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 135 (cols. 919–942C). The life presents Wenceslaus's conversion and rule as a work of divine grace, argues against Boleslav and pagan courtiers who offered sacrifice to alien gods, and treats baptism as regenerating the convert and the Christian ruler as bound to serve God above secular rank.
b.s: His Vita Vencezlavi is an early Latin account of St. Wenceslaus of Bohemia, framing the Slavic conversion as divine grace transmitted through written ecclesiastical tradition.

b.bio: Gundekar II, also printed Gundechar or Gunzo, was born 10 August 1019, educated at the Eichstätt cathedral school, and served as a canon there before becoming chaplain to Empress Agnes. Through her influence Henry IV named him bishop of Eichstätt in 1057; he held the see until his death on 2 August 1075. He devoted himself to diocesan affairs, especially clerical education, prepared for his clergy a ritual and liturgical collection known as the Gundecarianum containing a catalogue of the bishops of Eichstätt that successors continued until 1697, consecrated more than a hundred churches, and was venerated as a blessed after miracles at his grave.
b.s: The work held here is his historical record of the bishops of Eichstätt (Liber pontificalis / Vitae Pontificum Eystettensium), which asserts that Gundekar was the eighteenth bishop of the see, records Willibald's death in 781 after thirty-six years' service, and treats election of a bishop by common consent of clergy and people.

b.bio: Gundulf was a Norman monk of Bec Abbey and of St Etienne in Caen, a friend, pupil and chamberlain of Lanfranc, whom he followed to England in 1070 to help reorganize English monasticism after the Conquest. At Lanfranc's instigation he was appointed Bishop of Rochester in 1075, consecrated on 19 March 1077, and served until his death on 7 March 1108. He is remembered chiefly as a builder — Rochester Cathedral and Priory, the White Tower of the Tower of London, and castles at Rochester and Colchester are credited to him. The library holds his letters under PL 159.
b.s: His letters (PL 159), held by this library, are associated with his role as an episcopal administrator central to Lanfranc's post-Conquest reform of English monasticism.

b.bio: Gunther (Gunthar) belonged to a noble Frankish family and was consecrated Archbishop of Cologne on 22 April 850. He resisted ceding Bremen to Ansgar until Pope Nicholas I settled the matter around 860. As arch-chaplain to King Lothair II, he led the Aachen synods of 860 that compelled Queen Teutberga's confession and permitted the king to discard her. Gunther was excommunicated and deposed in 863. He died 8 July 873.
b.s: The works held here are his polemical letters and the 'Diabolical Chapters' defending the Lothair II divorce case against Pope Nicholas I, arguing that consent makes marriage, that promised faith must be kept, and that resistance to papal condemnation is justified — documents of the ninth-century conflict between episcopal synodal authority and the Roman see.

w: Letter to the Brothers of Reichenau

b.bio: Gunzo of Novara, a grammarian and deacon of the tenth century, is known chiefly for his Epistola ad Augienses, a reply to an invective against him by a monk of Saint Gall. The letter defends his learning and character before the monks of Reichenau, rivals of Saint Gall, and argues that bad speech corrupts morals. The library also holds a short Epistle to Atto. His death date and other offices are not given in the sources.
b.s: The Epistola ad Augienses is an important witness to late tenth-century intellectual culture and to classical doctrines linking style with character.

b.bio: The library holds under this name a single one-page 'Admonition' printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 99. None of The surviving records identifies this author. The sources instead describe three different men whose names resemble the entry: Gotthard Heidegger (1666–1711), a Swiss Reformed pastor and satirist of Zürich; Gottschalk of Orbais (c. 808–868), the Saxon monk condemned for teaching double predestination; and Gottfried von Hagenau (d. 1313), an Alsatian canon, physician and poet. None of these matches a Latin patristic author with a short admonitory piece in PL 99, so no dates, offices or biography can be asserted for the author as catalogued.
b.s: The single held work is a brief admonition preserved in PL 99; its attribution remains unresolved on the evidence available.

b.bio: Godefridus Henschenius (Godfrey Henschen or Henskens) was born at Venray in Limburg on 21 June 1601, son of the cloth merchant Henry Henschen and Sibylla Pauwels. He studied at the Jesuit college of 's-Hertogenbosch, entered the Society of Jesus at Mechelen on 22 October 1619, taught Greek, poetry and rhetoric at Bergues, Bailleul, Ypres and Ghent, and was ordained priest on 16 April 1634. Sent to Antwerp in 1635, he became Jean Bolland's collaborator on the Acta Sanctorum and was admitted to the profession of the four vows on 12 May 1636. His commentary on the Acts of St Amand fixed the method of the whole undertaking. With Daniel van Papenbroeck he made a literary journey through Italy, France and Germany from 22 July 1660 to 21 December 1662. He died at Antwerp on 11 September 1681.
b.s: The library holds his preliminary commentary to Peter Damian's works in PL 144, a historical and polemical survey defending Damian's cult for the Benedictines and the Avellana hermits' claim on him against rival attributions and opponents such as Ciaconius, Wion, Calvisius and Schmidius.

b.bio:
Heraclides Cappadociae (unknown) — The library records this author as 'Heraclides Cappadociae' with one work held, a 'Copy of a Letter' printed in PL 73. No surviving record concerns this person: surviving records describe Heraclides CYPRIUS, bishop of Ephesus, a native of Cyprus, monk of Scetis under Evagrius, deacon to John Chrysostom, ordained bishop of Ephesus c. 401 after the deposition of Antoninus, and summoned at the Synod of the Oak in 403 on charges including Origenizing views. Since the printed name differs ('Cappadociae'), these sources cannot be assumed to describe the author of the work held here, and no biographical claim about 'Heraclides Cappadociae' can be made from them.

Hervet, Gentian (1499–1584) — Gentian Hervetus (Hervet), born at Olivet near Orléans, was a French theologian, humanist, and controversialist. After studying at Orléans he tutored in Paris, then followed Thomas Lupset to England and entered the household of Cardinal Reginald Pole in Rome, where he translated Greek Fathers into Latin, including Clement of Alexandria, John Chrysostom, Theodoret, Palladius, and Nicholas Cabasilas. He was secretary to Cardinal Cervini (later Marcellus II), accompanied him to the Council of Trent in 1546, delivered an oration there against clandestine marriages, was ordained priest in 1556, became Vicar-General of Noyon, and received a canonry at Reims, preaching against the Calvinists.
