b.s: The single work held here (PL 73) argues that God alone is unteachable while all creatures are teachable, that true doctrine is a virtue of morals rather than of words, and that the soul must learn or teach or else be defective.

b.bio: None of The surviving records describes the author of this text. They cover three unrelated men named Girolamo Rossi: a Ravenna physician and historian (1539–1607), an eighteenth-century Roman antiquarian (1682–1762?), and a sixteenth-century Bishop of Pavia (1505–1564). None fits a Latin work printed in PL 144 alongside Peter Damian material. The library record alone identifies this Rossi as the writer of a short fourth Life of Peter Damian, defending Damian's reform causes against the Milanese clerics and the antipope Cadalus.
b.s: The work held here is a brief hagiographical and polemical Life of Peter Damian that treats simony, clerical concubinage, the Roman primacy, and the Cadalus schism from Damian's circle's standpoint.

b.bio: Born at Imola in 1464 as Lodovico Zarrabini di Cotignola's son, he took the name Flaminio during his humanist formation and studied at Bologna under Filippo Beroaldo. He taught belles-lettres at Serravalle, Montagnana, Vicenza, Imola, and finally Bologna, losing his property after Venice's defeat by the League of Cambrai and declining Julius II's invitation to Rome. Widowed late in life, he took vows and became a prior, dying at Bologna on 18 May 1536. He was father of Marcantonio Flaminio (1498–1550). A poet, prose writer, and translator from Italian into Latin, he also rendered Pietro Aaron's Libri tres de Institutione Harmonica into Latin.
b.s: The single work held here, a six-page second Life of Peter Damian printed in PL 144, is attributed to him by the library's shelf, but its content — an eleventh-century monastic vita citing Romuald, Stephen IX, and Alexander II, and polemicizing against Milanese clergy and a deceased archbishop of Ravenna — cannot plausibly be his work; readers should treat the shelf attribution as erroneous or at least highly doubtful.

w: Dissertation on the Date and Doctrine of Tertullian

b.bio: Benedictine patristic writer born at Füssen in Bavaria on 6 February 1747; died 8 March 1800 at the Abbey of St. George in the Black Forest (Hefele says 1801). He made solemn profession in 1764 and was ordained priest in 1771, then spent his life at Villingen as director of the gymnasium, professor of church history and dogmatic theology, and finally prior. His major work was the Historia theologico-critica de vita, scriptis atque doctrina SS. Patrum aliorumque scriptorum eccl. trium priorum sæculorum, thirteen volumes published at Augsburg between 1783 and 1789. The dissertations and prolegomena held here are drawn from that survey of the writers of the first three centuries.
b.s: The works here are his critical dissertations on Tertullian and related early authors, dating texts such as De oratione and Ad martyres to before Tertullian's Montanist defection and denying him authorship of the Acts of Perpetua, against Hoffmann, Tillemont, Pamelius, and Whiston.

b.bio: Joannes Franciscus Madrisius, styled Utinensis (of Udine) on the title page, edited the first collected edition of the works of Paulinus II, patriarch of Aquileia (d. 802), printed in Venice by Francesco Pitteri in 1737. The edition gathered previously published and unpublished texts ('ex editis ineditisque'), supplied notes and dissertations, and appended two collections of old documents. The library holds his general preface, a forewarning to the reader, a life of Paulinus, and dissertations defending claims about the Aquileian patriarchate — including that the schismatic patriarch was Paulinus rather than Paul, that Paulinus became patriarch in 776 not 774, and that Verona was subject to Aquileia.
b.s: His 1737 Pitteri edition remains the vehicle through which readers encounter Paulinus of Aquileia, and its dissertations engage Basnage, Pagi, Baronius, and the Adoptionist controversy of Felix of Urgell and Elipandus via Alcuin.

b.bio: The two Latin pieces held under this name — a short historical notice and an epitaph on one Guido, asserting that worldly honor is fleeting and that the humble soul outlives the rotting body — sit in the Patrologia Latina among medieval texts. No surviving record identifies their author or connects them to any documented bearer of this name. A well-documented Guillaume Marlot exists: a Benedictine monk, grand prior of Saint-Nicaise at Reims (born December 1596, died 7 October 1667), historian of Reims and continuator of Flodoard. His century, order, and known works do not match the contents or placement of the pieces held here, so he should not be assumed to be this author.
b.s: The works held here are minor occasional Latin pieces on the vanity of worldly honor; the famous Marlot of Reims historiography is probably a namesake, not their author.

b.bio: Born in Venice on 2 September 1707 and christened Nicola Giacomo, he entered the Camaldolese Order at San Michele di Murano in 1722, taking the name Gian Benedetto. He studied theology and philosophy at his order's houses in Florence and Rome, then taught before serving as confessor and archivist at Treviso and chancellor at Faenza (from 1747). Elected abbot of San Michele in 1760 and Superior General in 1765, he resided in Rome during his five-year term, favored by Pope Clement XIII, then returned to Murano as abbot until his death there on 14 August 1777.
b.s: His chief work is the Annales Camaldulenses ordinis S. Benedicti (9 vols., Venice, 1754–73), written with Anselmo Costadoni after the model of Mabillon; the single 'Admonition' printed under his name in PL 151 cannot be his, since that volume belongs to eleventh-century authors — the attribution appears to be a homonym or misattribution.

w: Dissertation for the Orthodoxy of SS. Perpetua and Felicity

b.bio: Born Agostino Francesco Orsi at Florence on 9 May 1692, he entered the Dominican Order at Fiesole on 21 February 1708, taking the name Giuseppe Agostino. He taught at San Marco, Florence, and from 1732 at the College of St. Thomas in Rome, then served as secretary of the Congregation of the Index (1738) and as Magister Sacri Palatii (1749). Clement XIII made him cardinal of San Sisto in 1759. His chief work was the Istoria ecclesiastica, written against Fleury's Gallican-leaning history.
b.s: The work held here is his dissertation defending the orthodoxy of SS. Perpetua and Felicity against Basnage's and Dodwell's claims that they were Montanists, arguing from Tertullian's silence, Pontius's attestation, and the martyrs' virtues that they died as Catholic martyrs.

w: Notice concerning Richer and his Chronicle

b.bio: Georg Heinrich Pertz was a German historian and librarian born in Hanover on 28 March 1795 and educated at the Georg August University of Göttingen. In 1823 Baron vom Stein enlisted him as editor of the Monumenta Germaniae Historica, the great edition of medieval German sources; he directed it for roughly half a century, during which twenty volumes of sources appeared under his editorship. He died in Munich on 7 October 1876 while attending a sitting of a historical commission and was buried in Berlin. The works held under his name in this library are not theological treatises but the editorial apparatus of Migne's Patrologia Latina: prefaces, admonitions to readers, and historical and literary notices introducing volumes of medieval chronicles and annals.
b.s: The works here are Pertz's prefaces and notices for PL volumes of medieval historians — including his notice establishing that Adam of Bremen wrote the Gesta pontificum, came from Upper Saxony, arrived at Bremen in 1068, was scholasticus by 1069, completed the work circa 1075, was learned in Greek, and was buried at Ramesloli convent — arguing throughout that the historian must ground claims in charters and earlier authors.

b.bio: Born at Gallarate on 23 November 1589 and died there on 17 November 1659, Puricelli was a priest, historian and antiquary specializing in medieval Milanese and Ambrosian history. He taught in the archiepiscopal seminary, served as arciprete of the collegiate church of San Lorenzo, and won notice for charity during the plague of 1630. A tireless collector of documents and manuscripts, he published the Ambrosianae basilicae ac monasterii monumenta (Milan, 1645) and left many works unprinted, including his researches on the Humiliati gathered for Cardinal Federico Borromeo, later used by Tiraboschi.
b.s: The dissertation held here is a citation-survey and polemic defending the tradition that Ambrose barred ordination to bigamists (not merely married men) and required clerical continence after ordination, arguing against Datius, Gualvaneus Flamma, Landulph the elder, Bernardino Corio, and engaging Bellarmine and Baronius.

b.bio:
George Ridel (d. August 1189) — Geoffrey Ridel was an Angevin royal administrator who served as a royal clerk, witnessing charters by about 1156, and held the living of Woolpit from 1161. He succeeded Thomas Becket as Archdeacon of Canterbury in early 1163 and acted as Lord Chancellor from 1162 to 1173, also serving as a royal judge and baron of the Exchequer by 1165. A firm supporter of Henry II against Becket, he was sent to the papal curia at Sens/Rome in 1164 on the king's business and earned from Becket's party the nickname 'archidiabolus'. He was appointed Bishop of Ely in 1173 and ordained bishop on 6 October 1174.

James Malet (unknown) — The library holds a single dedication letter under this name in Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL 147), addressed to John, bishop of Avranches. The letter places this James Malet in eleventh-century Normandy, a contemporary of Bishop John of Avranches (John of Rouen). the surviving records describe other men of similar names — a Tudor canon of Windsor named James Malett (d. 1543), the Victorian novelist 'Lucas Malet', and the Scottish Latin scholar James Melvin — none of whom matches a work printed in PL 147, so they are set aside as homonyms and nothing is asserted from them.

Jean Prevot (unknown) — The library holds one item under this name: a dedication letter printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina, volume 147, addressed to John, bishop of Avranches. the surviving records describe other men named Prévost/Prevost or Garnier — a twentieth-century French writer and Resistance member, Pope Leo XIV (Robert Francis Prevost), and the Jesuit Jean Garnier — none of whom matches an eleventh-century Latin author in PL 147, so they are set aside. Nothing in the sources establishes dates, offices, or biography for this Jean Prevost.
b.s: The library holds only his dedication letter (PL 147), addressed to or citing John, bishop of Avranches; his importance here is documentary rather than theological.

b.bio: The library prints this name as 'Saxe'; the author is Giuseppe Antonio Sassi (Latin: Saxius), born and died in Milan. A Catholic priest of the Oblates of Saints Ambrose and Charles, he took his doctorate at the Ambrosian College, was appointed rector there in 1711, and served as curator of the Biblioteca Ambrosiana founded by Cardinal Federico Borromeo. He worked on medieval Milanese history, contributed notes and manuscript transcripts to Muratori's Rerum italicarum Scriptores, and revised Sigonius's De regno Italiae.
b.s: His standing rests on scholarship around the Ambrosian rite; the work held here is a Prolegomena printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 173.

b.bio: No source identifies this Josephus Maria Scaresius with dates, offices, or institutions, and the library record does not supply them. The name as printed here should not be confused with Joseph A. Scares, a modern sociologist of religion, or with Josephus Adjutus (c. 1602–1668), the Assyrian theologian active at Wittenberg; neither matches the work held. What the record shows is a single prefatory piece, 'To the reader,' printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 2 among the works of Tertullian.
b.s: The piece held here is an editorial preface arguing for the genuineness of a fragment attributed to Tertullian, citing Bede and contemporary Roman authorities including Francesco Barberini, Felice Contelori, and Pope Urban VIII.

b.bio: No surviving record identifies this person. The library holds only a censor's approval printed under the name Gisbertus Spechtius in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 152, which indicates he examined and approved a work for publication; the approval itself is the sole trace of him here. the surviving records describe three different men — Blaise Gisbert, a French Jesuit rhetorician (1657–1731); Jean-Baptiste Specht, a nineteenth-century Alsatian theologian; and Gisbertus Voetius, the Dutch Reformed theologian — none of whom matches the name or period of this record, so they are set aside.
b.s: His appearance in this library is limited to a formal censor's approval in PL 152, useful chiefly as evidence that the approved work passed ecclesiastical review.

b.bio: None of The surviving records describes a Gabriel de Treio: they cover Gabriel Bucelin (Benedictine, 1599–1681), Cardinal Gabriel Trejo y Paniagua (1562–1630), Gabriel de Vergara (Franciscan missionary), and Gabriel de La Ribourde (Recollet) — different men in different centuries and traditions, and none is credited with the work held here. The author is therefore known only through the letter itself. It is addressed to Francisco Bivarius and defends the antiquity and dignity of Spanish Christianity against slander of Spain's ecclesiastical fame.
b.s: His single surviving letter is an early polemic for apostolic origins of Spanish Christianity, marshalling Tertullian, Cyprian, Cyril, and Flavius Lucius Dexter against infidels, heretics, and deniers of episcopal dignity.

b.bio: Georg Waitz, born at Flensburg and educated at Kiel and Berlin, was a historian of the Ranke school. He joined Georg Heinrich Pertz on the Monumenta Germaniae Historica in 1836, held chairs at Kiel (1842–1848) and Göttingen (1849–1875), sat as a deputy of the Frankfurt Nationalversammlung, and from 1875 chaired the MGH Zentraldirektion while leading its Scriptores section. The pieces under his name here are not patristic texts but nineteenth-century editorial apparatus: prolegomena, prefaces, notices, and historical introductions he wrote for Migne's Patrologia Latina volumes, chiefly introducing Burchard of Worms, the Annals of Saint-Bénigne de Dijon, and related medieval authors.
b.s: A reader meeting Waitz in these volumes is reading the critical introductions of a leading nineteenth-century editor of medieval sources, not an ancient author; his notices supply the manuscript history and bibliographic grounding for the texts they precede.

b.bio: The library prints this name over a two-page legal text in PL 138 treating the civil magistrate and the church: bishops and counts jointly enforce the peace, negligent counts forfeit office, laymen owe military aid when summoned, and charters stand by oath of notary and witnesses. No surviving record identifies an author of such a work. Three medieval men named Guy appear in the sources — Guy of Bazoches, canon of Châlons-sur-Marne (d. 1203), chronicler of the Third Crusade; Guy, bishop of Amiens (d. 1075), poet of the Carmen de Hastingae Proelio; and Gregory of Tours, who is not a Guy at all — and none matches these laws.
b.s: The work held here is a fragment of Frankish peace-keeping law binding episcopal and comital authority together, not writing by any of the sourced Guys.

b.bio: Surviving records do not clearly identify this author; they concern Guy of Bazoches (d. 1203), Guy bishop of Amiens (d. 1075), Guy of Merton, and Guido de Monte Rochen — different men with similar names, and none matches a monastic letter on simony printed in PL 151. What is known comes from the library record alone: a Latin ecclesiastical writer called Guy the Monk, represented here by a single letter addressed to Heribert.
b.s: The letter to Heribert is a polemic asserting that simony is the first and worst heresy corrupting the church, that simoniac ordination makes the ordinand a heretic and no true priest, and that communicating with such heretics incurs excommunication; it also holds that silence in face of a brother's peril is fratricide and that masses of excommunicate heretics provoke God's wrath.

b.bio: Georgius Lapitha (Geōrgios Lapithēs) was a fourteenth-century Greek Cypriot writer and landowner, probably named for the town of Lapithos. His property funded scholarly pursuits and the ransoming of Christian captives from the Turks, and his residence hosted intellectual debate with visiting scholars. He was a prolific translator — David Pingree credits him as likely translator of the Toledan Tables from Latin into Greek — and is also described as a theologian opposed to the Hesychasts, philosopher, poet, philologist, and astronomer. Few of his works survive; Pinakes lists Canones de septem sacramentis, an Epistula ad Nicephorum Gregoram, and Versus.
b.s: The library holds a short moral-theological text (PG 149) arguing that self-knowledge obliges man to live for eternity, that the soul is an incorporeal immortal image of God, and that the same body will rise incorruptible.

b.bio: A Byzantine theologian of Bulgarian origin, born at Prilep, who studied in Thessaloniki under Thomas Magistros and Gregory Bryennios. A pupil of Gregory Palamas, he first mediated between Palamas and Barlaam of Calabria in the dispute over the Uncreated Light, but from 1341 turned against Palamas, denouncing his doctrine as Messalianism. He was excommunicated at the Council of Constantinople in 1347 and died in exile, apparently a victim of the plague of 1348. He held that God's uncreated energy is identical with the divine essence, not distinct from it.
b.s: The principal opponent of Palamite Hesychasm in its first phase; the work held here defends divine simplicity and attacks the Palamite doctrine of the light as heretical Messalianism.

b.bio: Born in Constantinople around 1355, Plethon studied there and at Adrianople, then settled at Mistra in the Peloponnese, where he taught and served as a consultant to Emperor Manuel II Palaeologus, composing proposals for social and governmental reform. A professed Platonist who wrote commentaries on Aristotle's logical works, he argued that Aristotle denied creation because he held the world eternal. At the Council of Florence (1438–39) he was designated one of the six champions of the Orthodox Church against the Latins. His last work, the Nomoi or Book of Laws, circulated privately among close friends, rejected Christianity for a return to worship of the classical Hellenic gods blended with ancient wisdom based on Zoroaster and the Magi. Sources give his death as 1450/52 at Mistra (Britannica) or 1452/54 at Mystras (Wikipedia).
b.s: The works held here are his PG 160 writings: polemics for Plato against Aristotle on creation and the soul's immortality, treatises on virtue and providence, and speeches urging that the Peloponnesians are Hellenes by race and education whose recovery would restore imperial glory.

b.bio: Gregory V was born Bruno of Carinthia, son of Duke Otto I of Carinthia and Judith, a member of the Salian dynasty and relative (cousin) of Emperor Otto III, who had him elected pope after the death of John XV; he was consecrated on 3 May 996 and crowned Otto III emperor later that month (21 May per the Catholic Encyclopedia). Sources disagree slightly on his birth year (c. 970 or 972) and his death day in early 999 (18 February per Wikipedia; 4 February per the Catholic Encyclopedia; 'February or March' per Encyclopedia.com). Driven from Rome by Crescentius in the fall of 996, he returned with imperial forces in February 998, when Crescentius was executed and the antipope John XVI was deposed. His surviving letters are chiefly privileges that exempt monasteries from secular jurisdiction and confirm the free election of abbots, along with a privilege for Cambrai and the acts of the synod at Pavia that restored Arnulf to Reims and condemned Gerbert as an intruder.
b.s: His surviving letters show an Ottonian papacy asserting papal privilege, monastic immunity from secular jurisdiction, and supreme pastoral care over all churches against metropolitans and royal interference.

b.bio: Teobaldo Visconti of Piacenza, archdeacon of Liège from 1246, was elected pope on 1 September 1271 at the end of the longest papal election in history (1268–1271), during which the cardinals at Viterbo were confined and their food curtailed to force a decision. He was not a cardinal and was only ordained priest on 19 March 1272 and consecrated bishop on 27 March 1272, after his election. He convened the Second Council of Lyon and issued conclave regulations that remained standard until the twentieth century. He was beatified in 1713.
b.s: The work held here, the Roman Order XIII, is a liturgical text on papal ordination whose theses—that concordant cardinal election makes the pontiff, that an elected but unconsecrated pope may not celebrate mass, and that consecration completes what election begins—bear directly on Gregory X's own case as a non-priest elected pope.
